paragraphs.heading: What magma is
paragraphs.text: Magma is natural material, molten or semi-molten, and all igneous rocks form from it. It is found beneath the surface of the Earth, and people sometimes call it lava in casual speech, which is incorrect. It is liquid rock that usually carries suspended solid crystals. As magma nears the surface the overburden pressure falls and dissolved gases bubble out of the liquid, so magma near the surface has solid, liquid and gas in it.

paragraphs.heading: Where it comes from and goes
paragraphs.text: Magma is produced when the mantle or the crust melts. On Earth this happens in tectonic settings such as mid-ocean ridges, hotspots, subduction zones and continental rift zones. The melts move upward through the crust. There, geologists think, they are stored in magma chambers or in crystal-rich mush zones. After rising, magma may feed a volcano and come out as lava, or it may solidify underground as an intrusion such as a dike or a sill.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting magma by silica
paragraphs.text: A silicate magma is a molten mixture made mostly of oxygen and silicon, the two most abundant chemical elements in the crust of the Earth. Viscosity, temperature and many other properties of a magma are seen to go along with its silica content. On that basis silicate magmas are divided into four chemical types: felsic, intermediate, mafic and ultramafic.

paragraphs.heading: Felsic magma
paragraphs.text: Felsic magmas have more than 63% silica. With so much silica they are extremely viscous, from 10⁸ cP for hot rhyolite magma at 1,200 °C to 10¹¹ cP for cool rhyolite magma at 800 °C. Water, for comparison, has a viscosity of about 1 cP. Being so viscous, felsic lavas usually erupt explosively and leave deposits made of fragments.

paragraphs.heading: Peanut butter and ketchup
paragraphs.text: Intermediate magmas hold 52% to 63% silica. A typical viscosity is 3.5 million cP at 1,200 °C, slightly more than smooth peanut butter. Mafic, or basaltic, magmas have 52% to 45% silica and generally erupt at 1,100 to 1,200 °C. Their viscosity can be around 10⁴ to 10⁵ cP, similar to ketchup. Basalt lava is fluid and flows a long way from the vent, so it tends to build low-profile shield volcanoes or flood basalts.

paragraphs.heading: The hottest magmas
paragraphs.text: Ultramafic magmas all have under 45% silica. One kind, komatiite, contains over 18% magnesium oxide and is thought to have erupted at 1,600 °C. Its viscosity may have been as low as 100 to 1000 cP, geologists think, similar to light motor oil. No modern komatiite lavas are known, because the mantle of the Earth is now too cool to produce highly magnesian magmas.

paragraphs.heading: Meeting magma directly
paragraphs.text: The study of magma has relied on watching it after it has turned into a lava flow. Magma has been met in place three times, during geothermal drilling projects. Two of those were in Iceland and one was in Hawaii.
